summary: I contrasts change of colour with III white shining. Loss of sight at PrS 71/124 follows chemical whitening; the verb itself need not mean become blind. No separate culinary, metallurgical or lime-making sense is necessary.

The single JL oven verse contrasts endpoint Infectum ḥowər with completed koḥawər. Quoting the former in Infectum retains the supplied German; the existing English ko-Preterit example is not rewritten.

Material-culture/80 d̥ḥawriwa and old-houses/12 ḥawriwa share the kiln-whitening endpoint frame. File the latter as Infectum-wa rather than introducing a box on a-vocalism alone. Lahdo's prospective gәdḥawro shows a-vocalism is not sufficient to identify Preterit.
Old-houses/14–15 kḥawri/kḥawro remain provisionally in the reader's ko-Preterit category, but no new boxed examples are published until the process/result distinction can be confirmed.
94/527 is already an existing Infectum example. Its supplied German alignment is flagged as partial and malformed; it is not quoted as new translated evidence.

Confirm the speaker paradigm for ḥawriwa and kḥawri/kḥawro: does the latter represent ko-Preterit or ordinary Infectum with dialectal a? The provisional ko-Preterit occurrence decisions do not justify an added example.
Supply the complete aligned German ending for 94/527. The provided alignment warning and broken clause prevent quoting it as a new example; no replacement translation was invented.
The MAC kiln excerpt has 'the became really white'; this edition wording is preserved. Confirm the English typo during editorial review.
Whitening applies to oven, vessel, sugar-coated food, lime stones, hair, eyes and linen; these participants and physical causes do not establish new meanings.
White shining extends from teeth to a castle and a bone; III is intransitive in all these occurrences, despite its derived-stem form.
